                          RESPONSE BRIEF OF GERONIMO POWER, LLC

        Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”)

December 18, 2025 order1 and the Commission’s January 23, 2026 Notice of Extension of Time,2

Geronimo Power, LLC (“Geronimo Power”) hereby submits this response brief.3

I.      INTRODUCTION

        The current paradigm for serving large loads in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) is

not sufficiently flexible to accommodate the growth of hyperscale data centers and other large load

customers that have the capability to meet their demand—in whole or in part—using co-located

generation resources. At the same time, growing resource adequacy concerns within the PJM

             PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“Order”).

See NGV NGR Acquisition Co, LLC, Docket No. EC25-64-000, Notice of Consummation (June 9, 2025).

                                                          1
 region have increased the importance of ensuring that market rules provide an incentive for large

loads to pursue supply arrangements that mitigate their impact on the grid and other customers.

Maintaining existing barriers to co-location and other “bring your own generation” solutions has

the potential to lead to higher prices for ratepayers, a less reliable grid, and put at risk America’s

place at the forefront of the global economy.

       Geronimo Power applauds the Commission for recognizing that this outcome is

unacceptable and ordering PJM to reform existing market rules to provide large loads with the

flexibility necessary to pursue arrangements that allow these customers to receive service on a

timely basis, minimize their reliance on the transmission system, and, ultimately, reduce costs for

other ratepayers within the PJM region. The Commission’s recognition that the PJM tariff must

include transmission service offerings that reflect the use of the grid by co-located loads will, if

properly implemented, ensure that co-located loads can come online more quickly and avoid

triggering unnecessary transmission infrastructure upgrades.4 The Commission’s requirement that

PJM allow co-located load to select from two new types of transmission service—a Firm Contract

Demand transmission service and a Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service—is a key

part of this framework and represents an important first step in ensuring that co-located loads have

the option of taking transmission service that is consistent with their actual impact on the grid.

       Geronimo Power believes that certain proposals outlined in the initial brief filed by the

PJM Transmission Owners run counter to the objectives outlined in the Commission’s order in

this proceeding and will result in charges that do not reflect co-located loads’ actual impact on the

grid, disincentivize large loads from co-locating with new generation resources, and ultimately




       4
           Order at P 162.

                                                  2
 extend the status quo in PJM that the Commission has found to be unjust and unreasonable.5

Specifically, the PJM Transmission Owners have proposed to use the same Firm Contract Demand

transmission service rate—which will be the same rate as Network Integration Transmission

Service (“NITS”)6—for purposes of establishing the rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand

transmission service despite the fact that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service is a

lesser service with lower curtailment priority.7 The PJM Transmission Owners have also proposed

to apply a significant, but vaguely defined “Grid Reliance Charge” that would apply to load being

served by co-located generation based on nebulous benefits that the PJM Transmission Owners

claim that all loads derive from the grid.8

        The Commission should reject the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal to set the Non-

Firm Contract Demand transmission service rate equal to the rates for firm service and establish

the proposed Grid Reliance Charge. While Geronimo Power acknowledges that co-located load

should pay for the transmission service it uses and the actual benefits it receives from the grid, the

PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed rates and charges have not been tailored to reflect the nature

of the service being provided. If approved, the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed rate for Non-

Firm Contract Demand transmission service and the Grid Reliance Charge will result in co-located

load paying rates that do not accurately reflect the services being provided and will create a

disincentive for large loads to pursue efficient co-location arrangements that have the potential to

support the reliability of the grid, avoid unnecessary transmission investments, and drive costs

down for ratepayers.

Indicated PJM Transmission Owners to Paper Hearing Questions (Feb. 23, 2026) (“PJM TO Brief”).

 II.      THE RATES PROPOSED BY THE PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS ARE NOT
         JUST AND REASONABLE

         A.       The PJM Transmission Owners Have Not Demonstrated That It Is Just And
                  Reasonable To Apply The Same NITS And Firm Contract Demand Rates To
                  Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service

         In its Order, the Commission required PJM to revise its tariff to offer co-located loads the

ability to take Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission services.9 The Commission

explained that the Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service would be a lesser service than

NITS or Firm Contract Demand transmission service since customers taking this service may only

do so “if transmission capacity is available” and this service is “curtailed during emergency

operations (i.e., it will be curtailed before existing firm transmission services and the new Firm

Contract Demand Transmission Service).”10 The Commission explained that this Non-Firm

Contract Demand transmission service may, for example, be used by a co-located load when the

resource that normally supplies it is expected to be offline for maintenance and the service is

reserved in advance.11

         Despite the fact that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service is a lesser service

than NITS or Firm Contract Demand transmission service and will have a lower curtailment

priority, the PJM Transmission Owners propose to charge co-located load for Non-Firm Contract

Demand transmission service at the same rate used for NITS and Firm Contract Demand

transmission service.12 There are numerous aspects of the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal



         9
            Order at P 2.
         10
             Id. at P 214. PJM has proposed that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service may only be taken
up to the MW level that a co-located generation resource is able to supply a co-located load; the portion of load that
is not supplied by co-located generation must take Firm Contract Demand transmission service. PJM Interconnection,
L.L.C., et al., Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al., Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. at 9 (Feb. 23, 2026) (“PJM
Brief”).
          11
             Order at P 214.
          12
             PJM TO Brief at 10.

                                                           4
 that are unclear.13 But when combined with PJM’s proposed requirement that an eligible customer

take Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service for the portion of its load served by co-

located generation,14 the implication of PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal appears to be that a

customer taking Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service would be required to pay a

transmission charge equivalent to the rate paid by customers taking firm service. Take the example

of 100 MW load co-located with a 100 MW generator located within a zone with a NITS and Firm

Contract Demand transmission service rate of $10,000/MW/year and a Grid Reliance Charge of

$2,580/MW/Year.15 Under the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal, the load would pay the same

amount if it reserved 100 MW of Firm Contract Demand transmission service or 100 MW of Non-

Firm Contract Demand transmission service. The only difference is that a portion of the rate paid

by the load electing Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service would be in the form of a

Grid Reliance Charge. This is illustrated in the table below, which builds on the examples included

in the PJM Transmission Owners’ brief.




         13
             For example, the PJM Transmission Owners indicate that the Grid Reliance Charge will be subtracted from
the Non-Firm Contract Demand service charge on a MWh basis for each MWh of Non-Firm Contract Demand
transmission service included in a transmission service reservation request. Id. at 10. This proposal appears to suggest
that the PJM Transmission Owners will charge for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service on a MWh basis.
Such a proposal would to be at odds with how transmission reservation charges are historically structured and the PJM
tariff. See PJM Tariff § 1 (Definitions – Reserved Capacity) (“‘Reserved Capacity’ shall mean the maximum amount
of capacity and energy that the Transmission Provider agrees to transmit for the Transmission Customer over the
Transmission Provider’s Transmission System between the Point(s) of Receipt and the Point(s) of Delivery under
Tariff, Part II. Reserved Capacity shall be expressed in terms of whole megawatts on a sixty (60) minute interval
(commencing on the clock hour) basis.”). The PJM Transmission Owners’ reference to charging on a per MWh basis
also appears inconsistent with other statements in their brief that contemplate assessing charges for Non-Firm Contract
Demand transmission service based on a customer’s reserved contract demand. See PJM TO Brief at 11 (discussing
the Non-Firm Contract Demand rate as applied on a MW/Year basis). If the Commission does not reject the PJM
Transmission Owners’ proposal outright, the Commission should, at minimum, require the PJM Transmission Owners
to clarify the nature of the rates and billing determinants that they are proposing.
          14
             PJM Brief at 9 (“To the extent that the gross demand of a Co-Located Load is not covered by the Eligible
Customer’s Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, the Eligible Customer must cover the remaining gross
demand by applying for Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service.”).
          15
             These are the same rates used by the PJM Transmission Owners in their brief to illustrate the application
of the new transmission services. PJM TO Brief at 7, 11.

        Charging a customer taking Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service the same

amount as a customer taking Firm Contract Demand transmission service is inconsistent with cost

causation principles and unjust and unreasonable. The Commission directed PJM to establish

Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service because it recognized that co-located loads may

not plan to withdraw energy on a regular basis and that these customers should have the ability to

“reserve transmission service . . . as needed during normal, non-emergency system operating

conditions.”17 Yet, under the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal, these loads will be required to

pay a rate equivalent to customers receiving a higher level of service that rely entirely on the grid

to serve their needs.

        The PJM Transmission Owners offer several rationales for charging co-located load taking

Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service the same rate for a lesser service, but none are

convincing. The PJM Transmission Owners start by asserting that charging customers taking Non-


        16
             This equals the Non-Firm Contract Demand Rate minus the Grid Reliance Charge. Although, as noted
above, it is not clear whether PJM will charge for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service on a MW basis.
          17
             Order at PP 214-215.

                                                      6
 Firm Contract Demand transmission service the same as they charge for NITS and Firm Contract

Demand transmission service is just and reasonable because the Commission has permitted non-

firm point-to-point (“PTP”) transmission service to be charged a rate no higher than the rate

charged for firm PTP transmission service.18 But just because the Commission has said that a rate

may not exceed a certain threshold, does not mean that setting the rate at that threshold is just and

reasonable. Indeed, when FERC adopted the principle that a non-firm rate may not exceed a firm

rate, it explained that “[i]n most cases, FERC expects that non-firm transmission rates will be

priced below the firm rate.”19 This is in fact the case in PJM where, as the PJM Transmission

Owners acknowledge, non-firm PTP customers receive a discounted rate as compared to firm PTP

customers.20

         The PJM Transmission Owners attempt to dismiss this evidence that non-firm service

should be, and often is, priced lower than firm service as something that is limited to customers

taking service at the PJM border and that should not be extended to a broader class of customers.21

The PJM Transmission Owners also assert that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service

is a superior service to non-firm PTP.22 But the PJM Transmission Owners are focusing on the

wrong issue. The issue is not whether co-located load should pay the same rate as non-firm PTP

customers in PJM. It is whether co-located load taking Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission

service should pay the same rate for this lesser service as NITS and Firm Contract Demand

customers pay. On this critical question the PJM Transmission Owners have provided no basis for



         18
            PJM TO Brief at 11.
         19
            Transmission Access Policy Study Group v. FERC, 225 F.3d 667, 731 (D.C. Cir. 2000). See also Northeast
Utils. Serv. Co., 57 FERC ¶ 61,340, 62103 (1991) (“A non-firm rate is generally lower than a firm rate to reflect the
nature of the interruptible wheeling service.”).
         20
            PJM TO Brief at 11, n.30.
         21
            Id.
         22
            Id. at 12.

                                                         7
 the Commission to conclude that requiring Non-Firm Contract Demand customers to pay more for

less is just and reasonable.

       The PJM Transmission Owners also argue that before they are required to “discount” the

rate charged for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service they must first “gather data” on

how Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service customers “are utilizing the service, taking

into account the intended purpose of the service, and the effect of that utilization on the system.”23

But there is no need for the PJM Transmission Owners to “gather data” to come to the conclusion

that charging the same rate for inferior service is not just and reasonable. And there is no exception

to the Federal Power Act’s (“FPA”) requirement that rates be just and reasonable while the PJM

Transmission Owners “gather data” to determine if a rate they have implemented is in fact a just

and reasonable rate. The PJM Transmission Owners must adopt a just and reasonable rate

beginning on the date they first offer Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service. They

cannot set an unjust and unreasonable rate based on superior services while they wait until they

gather more data to determine the extent to which such unjust and unreasonable rate should be

reduced when charging for an inferior service.

       If anything, the PJM Transmission Owners’ brief provides support for charging Non-Firm

Contract Demand customers a lower rate than is charged NITS and Firm Contract Demand

customers. The PJM Transmission Owners observe that the “historical purpose” of non-firm rates

being less than firm rates “is to encourage the efficient use of the transmission system – i.e., to

ensure that the system is being utilized optimally.”24 This makes sense. Allowing customers that

can limit their use of the grid to time periods when capacity is available to pay a lower rate for




       23
            Id. at 13.
       24
            Id.

                                                  8
 such non-firm service creates an incentive for customers to reduce their reliance on the

transmission system.

       Yet, the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal will undermine the incentive for large load

customers to reduce their reliance on the grid by applying the same rate to Non-Firm Contract

Demand transmission service as Firm Contract Demand transmission service.                The PJM

Transmission Owners’ failure to offer a Non-Firm Contract Demand rate that will not

disincentivize co-location arrangements and will encourage the efficient use of the transmission

system is contrary to a primary reason the Commission required PJM to adopt these new Contract

Demand transmission services: to avoid costly and inefficient transmission system buildout that

may not be necessary.25 To achieve this goal, the PJM Transmission Owners must adopt rates that

reflect the nature of the service being provided and encourage the efficient use of the transmission

system. The PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission

service rate does neither.

       The Commission should find that the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed Non-Firm

Contract Demand transmission service rate is unjust and unreasonable. Rather than starting from

the position that customers taking non-firm transmission service should pay the same rate as firm

customers, the PJM Transmission Owners should propose a Non-Firm Contract Demand

transmission service rate that includes a discount which reflects the non-firm nature of the service

they are providing.

       B.         Any Grid Reliance Charge Must Be Based On Demonstrated System Benefits

       Any charges imposed on co-located loads must be based on co-located load’s actual impact

on the grid and the transmission services they receive. The FPA requires as much. Specifically,



       25
            Order at P 160.

                                                 9
 the FPA’s just and reasonable standard incorporates a cost causation principle which requires that

the costs of providing a service be allocated to “those who cause the costs to be incurred and reap

the resulting benefits.”26 The cost causation principle prohibits the Commission from approving

a rate scheme that will result in one group of customers being required to pay for a service from

which they do not benefit.27 No amount of “emphasizing other competing interests permits FERC

to sacrifice the foundational principle of cost-causation by refusing to allocate costs ‘to those who

cause the costs to be incurred and who reap the resulting benefits.’”28

        The PJM Transmission Owners have not demonstrated that their proposed Grid Reliance

Charge reflects co-located loads’ actual impact on the grid and is consistent with the cost causation

principle. The PJM Transmission Owners explain that their proposed Grid Reliance Charge will

be applied to co-located loads based on “the difference between the amount of their firm contract

demand for Firm Contract Demand transmission service or, in the case of Non-Firm Contract

Demand Service customers, the amount of their reserved service, and their total (gross) on-site

load.”29 This means that, if this Grid Reliance Charge were to be implemented consistent with the

reforms proposed by PJM in this proceeding,30 it would effectively apply to any portion of co-

located load that was being supplied by a co-located generator. The PJM Transmission Owners

have proposed to apply this Grid Reliance Charge to co-located load being served by onsite

generation resources as a zonal charge based on the percentage of transmission depreciation and

            El Paso Elec. Co. v. FERC, 76 F.4th 352, 362 (5th Cir. 2023) (quoting Nat'l Ass'n of Reg. Util. Comm’rs
v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277, 1285 (D.C. Cir. 2007)). See also Sithe/Independence Power Partners, L.P. v. FERC, 285
F.3d 1, 5 (D.C. Cir. 2002) (citing Alabama Elec. Cooperative, Inc. v. FERC, 684 F.2d 20, 27 (D.C. Cir. 1982)).
         27
            Constellation Mystic Power, LLC v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1028, 1050 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (citing Black Oak Energy,
LLC v. FERC, 725 F.3d 230 (D.C. Cir. 2013)).
         28
            El Paso Elec. Co. v. FERC, 76 F.4th 352, 363 (5th Cir. 2023) (quoting Nat'l Ass'n of Reg. Util. Comm’rs
v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277, 1285 (D.C. Cir. 2007)).
         29
            PJM TO Brief at 14.
         30

                                                        10
 operations and maintenance expense of a transmission owner’s annual transmission revenue

requirement—which is currently 25.8 percent.31

       Given the significance of the Grid Reliance Charge—over a quarter of a PJM transmission

owner’s annual transmission revenue requirement—one would expect that the charge would be

tied to clearly defined benefits associated with the grid impact of a co-located load that is being

served by an onsite generator. But the PJM Transmission Owners have provided no such evidence.

Rather the primary basis for the Grid Reliance Charge appears to be “the inherent benefits that all

customers, including Contract Demand customers, receive as a result of their synchronization to

and reliance on the grid.”32

       Geronimo Power does not dispute that the grid may provide a benefit to co-located load

that generally does not rely on the transmission system for service and that it may be appropriate

to impose certain charges on co-located load for demonstrated costs they cause and benefits that

accrue to them. But the PJM Transmission Owners have not demonstrated that their proposed

Grid Reliance Charge bears any relationship to the service that will be provided to, or the benefits

received by, these co-located loads.

       As a starting point, the PJM Transmission Owners provide no detail on what sort of

“inherent benefits” will be provided to co-located load relying on an onsite generator to serve it.

The PJM Transmission Owners say that “Co-Located Loads are electrically connected to the

transmission system (not islanded) and therefore benefit from the system and should contribute to

the ongoing operation and maintenance of the transmission system, consistent with foundational

cost causation principles.”33 But not being islanded from the grid is not a benefit in and of itself.


       31
          PJM TO Brief at 14-15.
       32
          Id. at 14.
       33
          Id., Exh. PTO-0001 at 17:19-22.

                                                 11
 The PJM Transmission Owners have not articulated what the inherent benefit—that is separate

from the benefit co-located load will pay for as part of its Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission

service—that being connected to the grid provides.

        Besides unspecified and unidentified inherent benefits, the PJM Transmission Owners say

that the Grid Reliance Charge is “designed to reflect the costs of using the transmission system to

deliver black start and regulation services…”34 Geronimo Power does not disagree that co-located

load depends on and uses black start and regulation services. The Commission reached the same

conclusion in its Order.35 And PJM has proposed, as required by the Order, that it will assess

charges to co-located load on a gross basis for black start and regulation services.36 The PJM

Transmission Owners fail to adequately explain why the Grid Reliance Charge is appropriate given

that co-located load already will be paying separate charges for black start and regulation service.

        While the PJM Transmission Owners attempt to portray the Grid Reliance Charge as

necessary to account, in part, for the delivery of black start and regulation services, that is a

distinction without a difference. As the Commission observed in its Order, black start service is a

service that is provided by generators that have the ability to start without an outside electric

supply.37 All customers rely on black start generators to restart the grid following a blackout. But

black start service is not delivered like transmission service. Rather if the grid goes down, black

start generators are called upon to provide power to the grid to get it restarted. In fact, the PJM

tariff contemplates that black start units be located in certain locations and that they will “provid[e]




        34
           Id. at 14.
        35
           Order at P 209.
        36
           See PJM Brief at 27.
        37
           Order at P 185.

                                                  12
 Black Start Service at the identified locations.”38 Black start generators are not, as the PJM

Transmission Owners seem to imply, delivering black start service to discrete points on the grid.

         There also is no basis to conclude that there is a separate delivery cost associated with

regulation service. As with black start service, Geronimo Power agrees with the Commission that

it is appropriate to assess co-located loads on a gross basis for the costs of regulation service.39

Regulation service is essential for balancing the grid and even if co-located load never draws

energy from the grid regulation service may be necessary to balance changes in all load’s power

factor.40 But there is no basis to conclude that customers should be subject to a separate charge

associated with the delivery—to the extent regulation service can even be considered deliverable—

of regulation service. PJM measures the supply of regulation service on a zonal basis41 and

resources participating in PJM’s regulation market have no obligation to deliver this service to a

particular point on the grid.42

         Even if the PJM Transmission Owners were to demonstrate that there was a separate

delivery component to black start and regulation services—which, to be clear, they have failed to

do—they have not demonstrated that the rates proposed are not commensurate with the costs being

caused or the benefits received. Indeed, if there were costs associated with these services the PJM

Transmission Owners would be able to identify how charges for the delivery of black start and

regulation services are imposed on other transmission customers. Of course neither the PJM

Transmission Owners nor PJM point to such a charge. And they have provided no basis for the

to providing Black Start Service at the identified locations.”).

 Commission to conclude it is just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory to only impose a

black start and regulation-based delivery charge on co-located loads.

         The only other basis that the PJM Transmission Owners put forward for assessing co-

located loads that rely on their own generation a Grid Reliance Charge is that the PJM

Transmission Owners will incur “costs associated with the operations, maintenance, and other

activities” associated with the “increased number of protection schemes that will be required for

Co-Located Load customers.”43 Setting aside the fact that any costs associated with operating,

maintaining, and whatever other activities protection schemes require have not been shown to be

significant, the PJM Transmission Owners concede that such protection schemes will primarily be

the responsibility of co-located load themselves.44 Moreover, there is no reason to believe that any

costs that transmission owners will bear that are associated with these protection schemes could

not be addressed in interconnection agreements just as the costs for such facilities are currently

addressed in the interconnection agreement for generators.45

         The PJM Transmission Owners have failed to identify a single cost that provides a benefit

to co-located load that is not accounted for through other charges that will already apply to co-

located load or that may be addressed through an interconnection agreement. Aside from vague

 assertions of the inherent benefits the grid provides to co-located loads that rely on onsite

generation resources, there is no basis for the Commission to conclude that the PJM Transmission

Owners’ proposed Grid Reliance Charge is even “roughly commensurate”46 with the “burdens

imposed or benefits received” for the service provided to such co-located load.47 The Commission

should thus reject the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed Grid Reliance Charge as inconsistent

with the cost causation principle and unjust and unreasonable.

III.   CONCLUSION

       Geronimo Power respectfully requests that the Commission issue an order in this

proceeding consistent with this brief.
